newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Sabena downplays Swissair threat.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sabena downplays Swissair threat.

text.p: Swissair may write off its investment in loss-making Belgian airline Sabena this coming spring, but this is no prelude to a total pull-out by the Swiss carrier, Sabena's chief executive said on Tuesday.
"It might be that Swissair is going to write off its investment this spring. The formal decision is not yet taken," Paul Reutlinger told a meeting of the European Aviation Club.
"I want to make clear...this does not mean that Swissair is going out of this investment," said the burly Swiss, adding he was convinced that Sabena would not go bankrupt.
He warned however that the first six months of this year would be crucial for Sabena's future.
Last October he said Swissair was threatening to abandon its Sabena stake unless it started making profits soon.

Swissair paid six billion Belgian francs ($179 million) for its 49.5 percent stake in Sabena in 1995 but the Belgian airline's performance has remained below par since due to a series of strikes early last year which undermined passengers' confidence.
Swissair, which has an option to raise its stake in Sabena to about 60 percent after 2000, is seeking a return on capital employed of four percent in 1998 and eight percent in 2000.
Last October Reutlinger pushed through a savings plan which included job cuts, adjustments in flexibility and working conditions and a two-year wage freeze.
But he has made it clear to trade unions that despite the savings plan, Sabena might not recover from any new strikes.
Reutlinger also said that plans to relocate its pilots to a foreign country to avoid having to pay heavy Belgian social security levies would give the carrier more leeway.

"I'm absolutely convinced that, if naturally we take the right management decisions, if we have possibilities like outflagging of our flight crews, that Sabena has a very fair chance to survive and to be successful," Reutlinger said.
Pilots could be "flagged out" to Switzerland, which has an average income tax of 15 to 20 percent against 40 to 55 percent in Belgium or possibly Britain or Ireland.
Reutlinger said that Sabena held many trump cards, including the geographical location of the carrier's home base, Brussels.
"If I were not convinced that we are going to make it, I would not have accepted the job and instead stayed skiing in the Swiss mountains," said Swissair-appointed Reutlinger.
